It can reinforce trust among members, make sacrifice meaningful, bind individuals into shared purpose, and coordinate moral expectations through repeated practice. The chapter insists that such an evaluation, while not irrelevant, is incomplete. Religion also has to be understood as binding technology for collective life.

Haidt does not use that interpretation as a cheap debunking move. The point is not that religion is secretly nothing but tribal glue. The point is harder: religion has genuine moral and social force because it can coordinate people so effectively. It can elevate, discipline, and sustain them. Ritual and symbol can make a group feel larger than any single member. Shared obligations can stabilize commitment when private motivation weakens. Sacred language can deepen belonging by making ordinary cooperation feel morally weighty rather than merely useful. The chapter asks readers to take those powers seriously instead of dismissing them as accidental byproducts.

But the chapter also refuses innocence. The same structures that create solidarity can sharpen boundaries, intensify certainty, and reduce concern for outsiders. Once a community understands itself as coordinated under sacred significance, criticism can feel like betrayal and boundary defense can feel morally required. This is why religion becomes one of the strongest illustrations of binding and blinding together. The chapter does not ask readers to revere that double edge or to sneer at it. It asks them to see that the integrative strength and the narrowing risk are products of the same social machinery.

Placed near the end of the book, Chapter 11 functions as the institutional payoff of Part III. Earlier chapters explained moral intuition, moral plurality, groupishness, and the hive switch. Now readers can see one of the strongest human systems for repeatedly organizing those forces. Religion is therefore read less as an isolated truth-claim system and more as a durable practice of coordinated moral life. The warning is inseparable from the strength. The same structures that organize trust and solidarity can intensify certainty, sharpen boundaries, and narrow moral concern toward outsiders.
